body:
:host 127.0.0.1 と :family ipv4 を指定したサーバーの実際のソケットを lsof で確認。GNU は 127.0.0.1、remacs は *。family が非 nil の場合に bind_host を無条件で 0.0.0.0 に置き換えている。

対象: `29e7c960edec18a99107741c351d95444f8f6b18` / macOS / GNU Emacs 31.1 との同一再現コードによる比較。

## 再現手順

前提: ローカルソケットの bind/connect が許可された macOS 環境。

以下を `AUD-065.py` として保存する。

```python
import json, os, pathlib, select, subprocess, sys, tempfile, time
from pathlib import Path
ROOT = Path.cwd()
FORM = """(let ((s (make-network-process :name "audit-binding" :host "127.0.0.1"
               :family 'ipv4 :server t :service 0 :noquery t)))
  (unwind-protect (progn (message "AUDIT-BOUND") (sleep-for 30))
    (delete-process s)))"""


def inspect(binary, side, directory):
    proc = subprocess.Popen([str(binary), "-Q", "--batch", "--eval", FORM], cwd=ROOT,
                            stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    trace = b""
    try:
        deadline = time.monotonic() + 20
        while time.monotonic() < deadline and proc.poll() is None:
            if select.select([proc.stderr], [], [], 0.1)[0]:
                trace += os.read(proc.stderr.fileno(), 4096)
                if b"AUDIT-BOUND" in trace:
                    break
        if b"AUDIT-BOUND" not in trace:
            raise RuntimeError((side, "No readiness marker", trace))
        result = subprocess.run(["/usr/sbin/lsof", "-a", "-p", str(proc.pid), "-iTCP",
                                 "-sTCP:LISTEN", "-nP", "-Fn"],
                                capture_output=True, timeout=3)
        (directory / f"network-binding.{side}.out").write_bytes(result.stdout)
        (directory / f"network-binding.{side}.err").write_bytes(trace + result.stderr)
        addresses = [line[1:].rsplit(":", 1)[0] for line in result.stdout.decode().splitlines()
                     if line.startswith("n")]
        if result.returncode != 0 or len(addresses) != 1:
            raise RuntimeError((side, "Expected one listener", result))
        return json.dumps(dict(actual_listen_host=addresses[0]), ensure_ascii=False)
    finally:
        if proc.poll() is None:
            proc.terminate()
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=3)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            proc.kill()
            proc.wait()


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='remacs-bind-repro-') as tmp:
    print(inspect(Path(sys.argv[1]).resolve(), 'repro', Path(tmp)))
```

```sh
python3 AUD-065.py /path/to/emacs-31.1
```

```elisp
(defun audit-net-server (&optional options)

         (append options '(:name "audit-net-server" :host "127.0.0.1"
                           :server t :service 0 :noquery t :filter ignore :sentinel ignore))))
```

## Summary

Three `invisible-p`/`buffer-invisibility-spec` divergences in remacs:

1. Spec entries with a cdr are ignored — `(foo . t)` should mark `foo`
   invisible *with ellipsis*:

   ```elisp
   (with-temp-buffer
     (insert "ab")
     (add-to-invisibility-spec '(foo . t))
     (put-text-property 1 2 'invisible 'foo)
     (invisible-p 1))
   ;; GNU: 2 (truthy)   remacs: nil
   ;; also fails via (setq buffer-invisibility-spec '((foo . t)))
   ```

2. A list-valued `invisible` property is only checked against its
   first element — GNU scans every element:

   ```elisp
   (with-temp-buffer
     (insert "ab")
     (add-to-invisibility-spec 'foo)
     (put-text-property 1 2 'invisible '(x foo))
     (invisible-p 1))
   ;; GNU: t   remacs: nil
   ```

3. `invisible-p` on a position before `point-min` signals
   `args-out-of-range`; GNU returns `t`:

   ```elisp
   (with-temp-buffer (insert "ab") (invisible-p -1))
   ;; GNU: t   remacs: (args-out-of-range -1)
   ```

`display-message-or-buffer` leaves `current-message` permanently set in
remacs; GNU clears it once the message is echoed in batch mode.


## Summary

Float→integer rounding error classes and `ldexp` saturation diverge:

```elisp
;; NaN: different error symbol entirely
(truncate 0.0e+NaN)   ;; GNU: (overflow-error)  remacs: (domain-error "NaN" 0.0e+NaN)
(floor 0.0e+NaN)      ;; same

(ldexp 1.0 most-negative-fixnum)  ;; GNU: 0.0        remacs: 1.0
```

## Summary

`add-variable-watcher`/`get-variable-watchers` differ from GNU:

```elisp
;; ordering — GNU pushes new watchers to the front
(let ((v 'x)) (add-variable-watcher v 'ignore)
              (add-variable-watcher v 'car)
              (get-variable-watchers v))
;; GNU:    (car ignore)
;; remacs: (ignore car)

;; GNU:    (ignore)
;; remacs: (ignore ignore)

;; defvaralias doesn't notify watchers
(let ((log nil)) (add-variable-watcher 'v (lambda (s n o w) (push w log)))
  (defvaralias 'v 'fill-column) log)
;; GNU:    (nil)   — watcher fires once with where=nil
;; remacs: nil     — never fires

;; buffer-local setq path asymmetry
(let ((log nil)) (add-variable-watcher 'fill-column (lambda (s n o w) (push w log)))
  (setq fill-column 42) (kill-local-variable 'fill-column) (list log fill-column))
;; GNU:    (nil 70)      — no notification for setq of a per-buffer variable
;; remacs: (((#<buffer *scratch*> 42 set)) 70)
```

```elisp
(describe-variable 'fill-column)
;; GNU:    "fill-column is a variable defined in ‘C source code’.\n\nIts value is 70\n\nColumn beyond which ..."
;; remacs: "fill-column’s value is 70\n\nNot documented as a variable.\n ..."
```

Function documentation works (`(documentation 'car)` returns the docstring), so only the variable side of the DOC-file/property mechanism is missing. GNU's `documentation-property` also lazily resolves the integer offset through `etc/DOC` and returns a fontified `substitute-command-keys`-processed string.

## Summary

`format-time-string` diverges from GNU in zone naming, time-spec arity, and flag/width modifier handling.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(format-time-string "%H %Z" '(0 0) 0)
;; GNU:    "00 UTC"
;; remacs: "00 +00"   ← ZONE=0 not named "UTC"

(format-time-string "%Y" '(1 2 3 4 5))
;; GNU:    "1970"     ← extra spec elements ignored
;; remacs: error "Invalid time specification"

(format-time-string "%5Y" '(0 0))
;; GNU:    "01970"    ← field width
;; remacs: "5Y"       ← '%' dropped, '5' treated literally

(format-time-string "%03d" '(0 0))
;; GNU:    "001"
;; remacs: "3d"

(format-time-string "%-" '(0 0))
;; GNU:    "%-"       ← dangling flag char preserved
;; remacs: "%"
```

GNU's `Fformat_time_string` implements the full strftime-style modifier grammar (`_-0^#` flags, field widths, `:`/`::`/`:::` for %z) and only inspects `(HI LO . PS)` of the time spec.
title: format-time-string: zone naming, extra time-spec elements, flag/width modifiers

## Summary

`mapatoms` over an abbrev table visits symbols in a different bucket order than GNU — `""` (the table's internal sentinel) comes first in GNU, last in remacs.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((at (make-abbrev-table)))
  (define-abbrev at "x" "y")
  (let (r) (mapatoms (lambda (s) (push (symbol-name s) r)) at) r))
;; GNU:    ("" "x")
;; remacs: ("x" "")
```

## Summary

`buffer-list` ordering differs from GNU: GNU puts ` *Minibuf-0*` first and orders by recency-of-selection; remacs uses a different order. Consequently `last-buffer`, `other-buffer`, and `bury-buffer` behave differently.

## Reproduction

```elisp
;; after (get-buffer-create "bl1") and "bl2":
(buffer-name (car (buffer-list)))
;; GNU:    " *Minibuf-0*"
;; remacs: "bl1"

(buffer-name (last-buffer))
;; GNU:    "bl2"     (last buffer in the list, i.e. oldest)
;; remacs: "bl1"

(eq (last-buffer) (car (last (buffer-list))))
;; GNU:    nil   ← last-buffer is NOT simply (car (last buffer-list))
;; remacs: t
```

GNU's buffer list is ordered by recency of selection (buffer.c `Fbuffer_list` walks `next_buffer` chain; ` *Minibuf-0*` and ` *load*` head it); remacs appears to order by creation or currentness differently. The missing ` *load*` buffer is tracked separately in #38.

`unintern` with a symbol argument removes the obarray entry matching the symbol's *name*; GNU removes the entry only when that exact symbol object is in the obarray.

```elisp
(let ((o (obarray-make)))
  (intern "a" o)          ;; interns a distinct symbol "a" inside O

  (intern-soft "a" o))
;; GNU:    a    ← O's own "a" symbol survives (unintern no-op)
```

## Summary

Closures store the whole surrounding `let` alist in remacs; GNU stores `(t)` when no free variables are captured. Both the printed `#[...]` form and `aref` on the env slot diverge.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(prin1-to-string (let ((x 5)) (lambda (y) y)))
;; GNU:    "#[(y) (y) (t)]"
;; remacs: "#[(y) (y) ((x . 5))]"

(let ((x 5)) (let ((f (lambda (y) y))) (aref f 2)))
;; GNU:    (t)
;; remacs: ((x . 5))
```

When the lambda *does* reference `x` both sides agree (`(aref f 2)` → `((x . 5))`), so this is specifically the un-captured-binding case: GNU's interpreted-env convention keeps `(t)` as the empty-scope marker where remacs stores the raw binding alist.
title: Closure env slot stores raw let alist where GNU stores (t)

## Summary

`make-category-table`/`standard-category-table` don't build GNU's internal bool-vector contents — remacs stores nil in slots where GNU keeps `#&128` bitmasks. `char-category-set` etc. still work, but the table's printed/internal shape differs observably.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(standard-category-table)
;; GNU:    #^[#&128"\0\0\0…" nil category-table #^^[3 0 nil … #&128"…@…\2\20\0" …]]
;; remacs: #^[nil nil category-table #^^[3 0 nil … #&128"…@…\2\20\0" …]]
;;         — first contents slot is nil instead of the bool-vector bitmap

(with-category-table (make-category-table) (category-table))
;; GNU:    #^[#&128"\0…" nil category-table nil #&128"\0…" …]   ← 128-char bool-vector per leaf
;; remacs: #^[nil nil category-table nil nil nil …]             ← empty
```

GNU `category.c` allocates each leaf of a category table as a `#&95`-sized bool-vector (`make_bool_vector`); remacs' `make-category-table` leaves the slots nil. `char-category-set` answers correctly anyway, so this is observable only when traversing the table raw (e.g. `map-char-table`, `aref`, print).

## Summary

Two syntax-table gaps:

1. `char-syntax` returns nil for non-Unicode internal codes (0x110000–0x3FFFFF) where GNU's standard syntax table covers them as word constituents (119 = `w`).
2. `matching-paren` ignores the paren match stored by `modify-syntax-entry` — returns nil instead of the matching character.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(char-syntax 4194176)   ; GNU: 119   remacs: nil
(char-syntax 4194303)   ; GNU: 119   remacs: nil

(let ((st (copy-syntax-table)))
  (modify-syntax-entry ?x "(y" st)
  (with-syntax-table st
    (list (char-syntax ?x) (matching-paren ?x))))
;; GNU:    (40 121)     — open-paren syntax + match 'y'
;; remacs: (40 nil)     — syntax recorded, match lost
```

GNU's `Fmatching_paren` (syntax.c) returns `SYNTAX_MATCH` from the syntax entry's match field; remacs records the open syntax but never stores/returns the matching char. ## Summary

`text-quoting-style` is not a special (dynamic) variable in remacs — `(special-variable-p 'text-quoting-style)` → nil (GNU: t). Under `lexical-binding`, `let`-binding it is lexical, so `format-message` ignores the override; GNU's DEFVAR_LISP definition makes it dynamically rebindable.

```elisp
;;; -*- lexical-binding: t -*-
(let ((text-quoting-style 'grave))
  (format-message "a \\`%s\\' b" "x"))
;; GNU:    "a \\`x\\' b"    (grave → verbatim)
;; remacs: "a \\‘x\\’ b"    (global curve style applies — let has no effect)

(let ((text-quoting-style 'straight))
  (format-message "a \\`%s\\' b" "x"))
;; GNU:    "a \\'x\\' b"    (straight → ASCII ')
;; remacs: "a \\‘x\\’ b"
```

## Summary

Two print-variable bugs in `prin1`/`print`:

1. Negative `print-length` truncates everything to `(...)`; GNU treats it as no limit.
2. `print-integers-as-characters` is ignored — integers always print numerically.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((print-length -1)) (prin1-to-string '(1 2)))
;; GNU:    "(1 2)"        remacs: "(...)"

(let ((print-integers-as-characters t)) (prin1-to-string 97))
;; GNU:    "?a"           remacs: "97"
(let ((print-integers-as-characters t)) (prin1-to-string '(97 98)))
;; GNU:    "(?a ?b)"      remacs: "(97 98)"
(let ((print-integers-as-characters t)) (prin1-to-string [97 98]))
;; GNU:    "[?a ?b]"      remacs: "[97 98]"
```

GNU `print.c` applies `Vprint_integers_as_characters` in `print_object` (ints in character range print as `?c`), and treats negative `print-length`/`print-level` as unlimited (depth/len only compared when `FIXNUMP` and `> 0`... in GNU, `print-length` < 0 means "print all"). remacs appears to clamp negative lengths to 0 and never checks `print-integers-as-characters`. Related: #51 (`float-output-format` ignored).
title: print-length < 0 truncates; print-integers-as-characters ignored

## Summary

`indent-for-tab-command` is a stub that always inserts a literal TAB — it never calls `indent-line-function`, so TAB in `emacs-lisp-mode` (and everywhere else) inserts a tab character instead of computing mode indentation.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer (emacs-lisp-mode)
  (insert "(defun f ()\nx)") (goto-char 13)
  (call-interactively 'indent-for-tab-command) (current-column))
;; GNU:    2   (lisp-indent-line → defun body indent)
;; remacs: 8   (raw \t to next tab stop)

;; GNU in detail:
;;   (if c\na → 5,  (let ((x 1))\nx → 2,   (dolist (e l)\nx → 2,
;;   (cond\n(a → 1, (save-excursion\nx → 2
;; remacs: every continuation indents to a multiple of tab-width (8, 16, 24).
```

Root cause: `src/lisp/prelude.el:1880` defines

```elisp
(defun indent-for-tab-command (&optional arg)
  "Indent the current line (inserts a tab in fundamental mode)."
  (interactive "P")
  (insert "\t"))
```

which shadows `indent.el`'s real definition — the prelude stub survives because `indent-line`/`indent-according-to-mode`/`calculate-lisp-indent` are all correct when called directly, only `indent-for-tab-command` bypasses `indent-line-function`. (`newline-and-indent` next to it is the real GNU version and works.)

Also small: `lisp-body-indent` lacks the defcustom `standard-value` property — `(get 'lisp-body-indent 'standard-value)` → nil where GNU returns `((funcall #'#[...] [2] 1))` — the variable is a `defvar` in remacs but a `defcustom` in GNU (indent.el).
title: indent-for-tab-command is a literal-TAB stub, ignores indent-line-function

## Summary

`skip-chars-forward`/`skip-chars-backward` don't honor `[:name:]` (and `[[:name:]]`) POSIX character-class syntax in the skip-set string — they treat the class text literally, so e.g. `"[:alpha:]"` only skips the literal chars `[`, `:`, `a`, `l`, `p`, `h`, `]`.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer (insert "abc")
  (goto-char 1) (skip-chars-forward "[:alpha:]") (point))
;; GNU: 4   remacs: 2   (skipped only the literal 'a')

(with-temp-buffer (insert "abc")
  (skip-chars-backward "[:alpha:]") (point))
;; GNU: 1   remacs: 4

(with-temp-buffer (insert "123")
  (goto-char 1) (skip-chars-forward "[:digit:]") (point))
;; GNU: 4   remacs: 1

(with-temp-buffer (insert "a b")
  (goto-char 1) (skip-chars-forward "[:space:]") (point))
;; GNU: 1   remacs: 2   (skipped 'a' — a literal member of "[:space:]")

(with-temp-buffer (insert "ABC")
  (goto-char 1) (skip-chars-forward "[:upper:]") (point))
```

## Summary

`lisp-el-font-lock-keywords-2`'s "\\= doc-string escape" keyword stores the wrong regexp in remacs — the prelude's folded copy substituted `(rx "\\\\=")`'s *input* string for its `regexp-quote`d *output*.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(car (nth 10 lisp-el-font-lock-keywords-2))
;; GNU:    "\\\\\\\\="   (regexp matching the 3-char text \\= )
;; remacs: "\\\\="       (regexp matching the 2-char text \=)
```

GNU's `lisp-mode.el` has `(,(rx "\\\\=") (0 'font-lock-builtin-face prepend))` — `rx` on the literal 3-char string `\\=` produces the regexp `\\\\=` (matches `\\=` text, the doc-string escape sequence). ## Summary

`char-width` (and `string-width` via `gnu_char_width`) returns 1 for non-Unicode internal character codes ≥ 0x110000 where GNU's `char-width-table` assigns width 2. remacs' own `char-width-table` holds the correct value (2), but `f_char_width` never consults it — it early-returns 1 for codes above Unicode.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(char-width 1310720)          ; GNU: 2   remacs: 1
(aref char-width-table 1310720) ;; both: 2   ← table is correct, function ignores it
(string-width (string 1310720)) ;; GNU: 2   remacs: 1
```

Range 1310720–1311471 (0x140000–0x1416EF) is the `indian-2-column`/`arabic-2-column` charset range that `lisp/characters.el` maps to width 2 via `map-charset-chars`/`set-char-table-range` — both char-width-tables carry the range, but `f_char_width` (`src/lisp/builtins/strfn.rs:5055`) has `u > 0x10FFFF → 1` and `char_width` (`src/buffer/primitives.rs:7960`) returns 1 for `mule_seq_code` proxies, bypassing the table entirely.

## Unicode の幅上書きでも再現

追加確認対象: `29e7c960edec18a99107741c351d95444f8f6b18`。同じ原因は Unicode の文字のカスタム幅でも発生する。

```elisp
(let ((char-width-table (copy-sequence char-width-table))) (set-char-table-range char-width-table 26085 5) (list (char-width 26085) (string-width "日日") (truncate-string-to-width "日日" 6)))
```

```text
GNU Emacs 31.1: (ok (5 10 "日"))
remacs:         (ok (2 4 "日日"))
```

<!-- remacs-audit-extra: unicode-custom-width -->
title: char-width ignores char-width-table for non-Unicode internal codes

## Summary

Process bookkeeping divergences:

1. Duplicate process names aren't uniquified — GNU appends `<1>`, remacs keeps two processes both named `x`.
2. `delete-process`'d processes remain in `process-list` — GNU removes them.

```elisp
       (make-process :name "x" :command nil)
       (process-list))

  (memq p (process-list)))

(condition-case e (make-process :command '("x")) (error e))
;; GNU:    (error "Missing :name keyword parameter")
;; remacs: (error "Process name not given")
```

`file-name-extension` with PERIOD non-nil returns nil where GNU returns the empty string for a trailing dot / dotfile.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(file-name-extension "/tmp/.a" t)
;; GNU:    ""
;; remacs: nil
```

GNU's `Ffile_name_extension` for "/tmp/.a" — the dot at the basename start with PERIOD → returns `""` (empty extension string), not nil. remacs returns nil, collapsing the "no extension" and "empty extension" cases.

`"a."` (trailing dot, no PERIOD) and dotfile without PERIOD behave; only the `PERIOD` + empty-extension corner differs.
title: file-name-extension returns nil instead of empty string with PERIOD

## Summary

`delete-char`/`delete-backward-char` clamp and partially delete when COUNT runs past the buffer bounds, instead of signaling `end-of-buffer`/`beginning-of-buffer` and leaving the buffer unchanged.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer (insert "abc") (goto-char 4)
  (condition-case e (delete-backward-char 99) (error e)))
;; GNU:    (beginning-of-buffer)      ← error, buffer untouched
;; remacs: nil                        ← silently deletes 3 chars

(with-temp-buffer (insert "abc") (goto-char 1)
  (condition-case e (delete-char 99) (error e)))
;; GNU:    (end-of-buffer)

  (condition-case e (delete-backward-char 99) (error e))
  (buffer-string))
;; GNU:    "abc"    ← atomic: error means no deletion
;; remacs: "bc"     ← deleted what it could
```

`buffer-string` returns a unibyte string even for multibyte buffers/content, where GNU returns a multibyte string. `buffer-substring` returns the correct multibyte string — only `buffer-string` drops the flag.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer (multibyte-string-p (buffer-string)))
;; GNU:    t
;; remacs: nil

(with-temp-buffer (insert "é") (multibyte-string-p (buffer-string)))
;; GNU:    t
;; remacs: nil

(with-temp-buffer (insert "é") (multibyte-string-p (buffer-substring 1 2)))
;; GNU:    t   remacs: t   ← buffer-substring is correct

;; remacs: ("\200" nil)
```

## Summary

`split-window` doesn't enforce `window-min-height` / frame size limits — remacs allows far more splits than the frame can hold, where GNU signals `"Window too small for splitting"`.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((w1 (split-window)) (w2 (split-window))) (length (window-list)))
;; GNU:    ERR:(error "Window #<window 1 on *scratch*> too small for splitting")
;; remacs: 4

(let ((n 0))
  (condition-case e
      (while t (split-window) (setq n (1+ n)) (if (> n 30) (error "stop")))
    (error (list n e))))
;; GNU:    (0 (error "Window #<window 1 on *scratch*> too small for splitting"))
;; remacs: (31 (error "stop"))   ← split 30+ times without a limit

(condition-case e (split-window (selected-window) 1) (error e))
;; GNU:    #<window 7 on *scratch*>    (explicit size 1 allowed when frame had room)
;; remacs: (error "Window #<window 1 on *scratch*> too small for splitting")
```

GNU's `Fsplit_window` → `window_min_size` check in window.c enforces `window-min-height` (default 4) against the parent; remacs' batch window model has no effective height constraint (or a huge fake frame), so splits never fail until the arg form itself errors. The direction of the limit also differs — remacs hit its own ceiling later at a different argument.
title: split-window never enforces window-min-height

## Summary

`insert-file-contents` with a non-nil REPLACE argument reports the wrong inserted-count in its return value when the buffer is non-empty: GNU returns `(FILENAME 0)`, remacs returns the file size.

```elisp
       (insert "P")
       (insert-file-contents "/tmp/f.txt" nil nil nil t))
;; GNU:    ("/tmp/f.txt" 0)
```

## Summary

Thread bookkeeping diverges from GNU in two ways:

1. Finished threads disappear from `all-threads` immediately — GNU retains dead/unjoined thread objects until GC.
2. `thread-signal` on the current/main thread does not deliver the signal — GNU quits (the signaled error fires), remacs returns nil.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((th (make-thread #'ignore "named")))
  (memq th (all-threads)))
;; GNU:    (#<thread named>)   ← finished thread still listed
;; remacs: nil                 ← reaped eagerly

(let ((th (make-thread #'ignore)))
  (setq th nil)
  (garbage-collect)
  (length (all-threads)))
;; GNU:    2     remacs: 1
```

GNU keeps finished thread objects in `all_threads` until they're garbage-collected (threads.c `Fall_threads`); remacs removes them on exit.

```elisp
(thread-signal (current-thread) 'quit nil)
;; GNU:    process quits (rc=255, "Quit" on stderr)
;; remacs: nil   ← signal silently dropped
```

GNU's `Fthread_signal` → `signal_or_quit` on the main thread signals `quit` immediately; remacs' implementation appears to ignore signals delivered to the current thread.
title: thread bookkeeping: finished threads dropped from all-threads; thread-signal to self ignored

## Summary

`take` with N ≤ 0 signals `wrong-type-argument listp` for strings/vectors where GNU returns nil.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(take -1 "abcde")
;; GNU:    nil
;; remacs: ERR:(wrong-type-argument listp "abcde")

(take 0 "abc")
;; GNU:    nil
;; remacs: ERR:(wrong-type-argument listp "abc")

(take -1 [1 2 3])
;; GNU:    nil
;; remacs: ERR:(wrong-type-argument listp [1 2 3])

;; GNU:    nil
;; remacs: ERR:(wrong-type-argument listp "")
```

When the buffer a match was performed in is killed, GNU unchains the match-data markers (they print as `#<marker in no buffer>` and positions become unavailable). remacs keeps the markers bound to the dead buffer with their old positions.

```elisp
(progn
  (with-temp-buffer
    (insert "abc") (goto-char 1)
    (re-search-forward "a\\(b\\)"))   ;; buffer killed on exit
  (match-data))
```

Fresh buffers' buffer-local variable state diverges from GNU — `mode-name` is nil instead of `"Fundamental"`, and several GNU buffer-local bindings don't exist at all.

```elisp
;; GNU:    "Fundamental"
```

GNU batch `-l FILE` wraps the load in a buffer named `" *load*"`, which appears in `(buffer-list)` while the file loads. remacs never creates it.

## Reproduction

A file loaded with `remacs -Q -l probe.el` where probe.el contains:

```elisp
;; GNU:    (... #<buffer  *load*> ...)

```

`kill-buffer` doesn't validate that its argument is a string-or-nil before looking it up — non-string args produce `(error "No buffer named X")` instead of GNU's `(wrong-type-argument stringp X)`.

```elisp
(condition-case e (kill-buffer 5) (error e))
;; GNU:    (wrong-type-argument stringp 5)
;; remacs: (error "No buffer named 5")

(condition-case e (kill-buffer t) (error e))
```

## Summary

`secure-hash` ignores its BINARY argument — it always returns the hex digest, where GNU returns the raw binary digest (unibyte string) when BINARY is non-nil.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(secure-hash 'sha256 "abc" nil nil t)
;; GNU:    "\272x\277\217\317\352AA@\336]..."  (32 raw bytes)
;; remacs: "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad"
```

## Summary

`object-intervals` doesn't support buffer objects, and `set-text-properties` leaves phantom all-nil intervals that GNU collapses away.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer
  (insert "hello")
  (put-text-property 1 3 'a 1)
  (object-intervals (current-buffer)))
;; GNU:    ((0 2 (a 1)) (2 5 nil))
;; remacs: nil            ← buffers unsupported
```

`define-key` accepts keys that are not vectors or strings — symbols, integers, lists, `t` — where GNU signals `wrong-type-argument` `arrayp`. For `nil`, remacs signals `sequencep` instead of GNU's `arrayp`.

```elisp
;; GNU:    (wrong-type-argument arrayp bad)
```

## Summary

Menu items defined during boot with a function-valued `:keys` property (backquote-spliced `,(lambda ...)`) end up with `:keys nil` in the stored keymap. GNU stores the byte-code/closure object. This affects `menu-bar-edit-menu`'s cut/copy/paste items and is visible in `accessible-keymaps` / `lookup-key` output.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((item (cdr (assq 'cut (cdr menu-bar-edit-menu)))))
  item)
;; GNU:    (menu-item "Cut" kill-region :enable ... :help "..."
;;                  :keys #[0 "\x08\203\n\0\t\203\n\0\302\207\303\207"
;;                          [cua-mode mark-active
;;                           "\\[cua-cut-handler]" "\\[kill-region]"] 1])
;; remacs: (menu-item "Cut" kill-region :enable ... :help "..."
;;                  :keys nil)
```

Same for `[menu-bar edit copy]` and `paste` — every `:keys ,(lambda ...)` in `menu-bar.el` (`lisp/menu-bar.el` ~line 585) reads `nil`.

Still `nil` under `REMACS_NO_ELC=1`, so the loss happens in the interpreted boot eval, not the `.elc` twin reader.

Post-boot, the identical form works:

```elisp
(defvar mymap (let ((menu (make-sparse-keymap "E")))
                (define-key menu [cut]
                  `(menu-item "Cut" kill-region
                              :keys ,(lambda () "k")))
                menu))
;; remacs stores :keys #[nil ("k") ((menu keymap #1 "E"))] — a real closure
```

So the boot-time `,(lambda () ...)` splice yields nil — likely the backquote unquote in the boot eval path (prelude/`boot_lib`, before `install_macros` binds the backquote macros post-load) doesn't evaluate the spliced form. The item structure itself is built fine, suggesting `\`` expansion runs but `,` evaluation produces nil.

## Secondary difference

Even post-boot, closure environments print differently:

```elisp
;; GNU:    #[nil ((if ...)) (t)]            ← env shows (t)
;; remacs: #[nil ((if ...)) ((menu keymap #1 "E"))]  ← captures let env
```

GNU prints a `(t)` marker env; remacs retains the captured let bindings.
title: menu-item :keys lambdas become nil during boot load

## Summary

Hash tables with `:test 'eq` treat floats as value-equal keys, so `gethash` finds entries that GNU misses. In GNU, floats are heap objects and `eq` is identity — `(eq 1.5 1.5)` is `nil` — so an `eq` table can never look a float key back up.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((h (make-hash-table :test 'eq)))
  (puthash 1.5 'v h)
  (list (gethash 1.5 h) (gethash (+ 0.0 1.5) h)))
;; GNU:    (nil nil)
;; remacs: (v v)

(let ((h (make-hash-table :test 'eq)))
  (puthash 1.5 'v h)
  (gethash 1.5 h))
;; GNU:    nil
;; remacs: v
```

`:test 'eql` correctly finds `1.5` in both implementations; strings and conses under `eq` behave correctly (lookup misses, as GNU). Only floats diverge.

## Analysis

remacs `eq` itself is correct — `(eq 1.5 1.5)` returns `nil`, same as GNU — so the `eq` hash is inconsistent with the interpreter's own `eq`.

`src/lisp/builtins/hashfn.rs` `eq_key` (~line 125):

```rust
Value::Float(f) => HashKey::Float(f.to_bits()),
```

hashes floats by their bit pattern — a *value* hash — under `HashTest::Eq`. For GNU parity an `eq` table must hash a float by object identity (pointer), like `eq_key` already does for `Cons`/`Str`/etc. (`eql_key`'s `HashKey::Float` arm is the correct place for value hashing — that one is right.)

Note `Value::Int` under `eq` is fine (fixnums are `eq`-by-value in GNU since they're immediates).
title: eq hash tables treat float keys as value-equal

## Summary

`text-char-description` produces wrong strings for raw/eight-bit characters: it collapses eight-bit chars (0x3FFF80–0x3FFFFF) to `"?"` and turns C1 chars (0x80–0x9F) into literal backslash-octal text, where GNU returns a string containing the byte/eight-bit character itself.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(text-char-description 4194176)   ; = (decode-char 'eight-bit 128)
;; GNU:    "\200"  (string whose aref 0 is the eight-bit char 4194176)
;; remacs: "?"

(text-char-description 4194303)   ; eight-bit 255
;; GNU:    "\377"
;; remacs: "?"

(text-char-description 128)       ; C1 char
;; GNU:    string containing raw byte 0x80
;; remacs: "\\200"                (literal backslash-octal text, 4 chars)
```

`decode-char 'eight-bit` itself returns the correct character — `(= (decode-char 'eight-bit 128) 4194176)` is `t` in both — so the defect is confined to the description printer.

## Source

`src/editor/mod.rs` `f_text_char_description` (~line 9184): the `0x80..0xa0` arm emits `format!("\\{:03o}", c)` text instead of the raw byte character, and the fallback arm uses `char::from_u32(c).unwrap_or('?')`, which yields `?` for all eight-bit chars (0x3FFF80+ exceed `char::MAX`).

GNU reference: `keymap.c` `Ftext_char_description` — eight-bit chars are pushed into a unibyte string as their byte.

## Related minor finding

`(unibyte-char-to-multibyte 4194176)` signals a different error than GNU:

```elisp
;; GNU:    (error "Not a unibyte character: 4194176")
;; remacs: (wrong-type-argument characterp 4194176)
```

`src/lisp/builtins/strfn.rs` `f_unibyte_char_to_multibyte` (~line 449) uses `wrong_type_mut("characterp", ...)` for out-of-range ints instead of GNU's `error "Not a unibyte character: %d"`.
title: text-char-description mishandles eight-bit and C1 characters

## Summary

`call-process` (and probably the related `call-process-region`/`process-file`/`shell-command` paths) drops stderr instead of folding it into the destination the way GNU does in batch.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer
  (call-process "sh" nil t nil "-c" "echo out; echo err >&2")
  (buffer-string))
;; GNU:   "out\nerr\n"
;; remacs: "out\n"          ← stderr lost
```

Compare `(call-process "sh" nil (list t "/tmp/err.txt") nil "-c" "...")` variants — GNU honors the `(t STDERR-FILE)` destination form; verify `call-process-region` stderr routing as well.

Also verify `process-file` and `start-process` similarly — the process code is in `src/lisp/process.rs`.
title: call-process drops stderr instead of folding it into the buffer

## Summary

Time-related bugs:

1. `current-time-string` ignores its ZONE argument — always formats in local time.
2. Lisp timestamps of the form `(TICKS . HZ)` are accepted in cases GNU rejects (`(0 . 0)` → "Invalid time specification" in GNU, treated as 0 in remacs), and GNU's 4/5-element `(HI LO US PS)`/`(SEC…)` list forms are rejected by remacs (`(float-time '(0 0 0 100))`, `(decode-time '(0 0 0 0 0))`).

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(current-time-string 0 t)` | `"Thu Jan  1 00:00:00 1970"` | `"Thu Jan  1 09:00:00 1970"` — local zone applied to UTC |
| `(current-time-string 0 "UTC0")` | `"Thu Jan  1 00:00:00 1970"` | `"Thu Jan  1 09:00:00 1970"` |
| `(current-time-string '(0 . 0) t)` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `"Thu Jan  1 09:00:00 1970"` |
| `(format-time-string "%Y" '(0 . 0))` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `"1970"` |
| `(decode-time '(0 . 0) t)` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `(0 0 0 1 1 1970 4 nil 0)` |
| `(decode-time '(0 0 0 0 0) t)` | `(0 0 0 1 1 1970 4 nil 0)` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` |
| `(float-time '(0 . 0))` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `0.0` |
| `(float-time '(0 0 0 0 100))` | `0.0` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` |
| `(time-less-p '(0 . 0) '(0 . 1))` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `nil` |
| `(time-equal-p '(0 . 0) '(0 . 1))` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `t` |
| `(time-to-days '(0 . 0))` | `(error "Invalid time specification")` | `719163` |

`format-time-string` directives themselves match GNU (tested `%Y`–`%:::z`, `%N` variants). Related: `emacs-uptime`/`emacs-init-time`/`current-cpu-time`/`current-idle-time` values differ (expected — wall-clock noise), but `current-time-string` zone handling and timespec validation are deterministic bugs.
title: current-time-string ignores ZONE arg; invalid time specs accepted

body:
## Summary

`file-name-completion` returns `t` instead of the common-prefix string for partial matches — `t` is only correct when the name is an exact match. `file-name-all-completions` includes `"./"` and `"../"` (GNU strips them) and its result ordering differs from GNU's raw-readdir order. `directory-files` with COUNT picks different entries than GNU.

## Reproduction

Directory contains `utf8.txt utf8bom.txt utf8crlf.txt utf16le.txt utf16be.txt sjis.txt …`:

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(file-name-completion "utf8" dir)` | `"utf8"` | `t` |
| `(file-name-completion "utf" dir nil)` | `"utf"` | `t` |
| `(file-name-completion "" dir)` | `""` | `t` |
| `(file-name-completion "b" dir pred)` | `"b"` | `t` |
| `(file-name-completion "nosuch" dir)` | `nil` | `nil` (ok) |
| `(file-name-all-completions "u" dir)` | `("utf8bom.txt" "utf16le.txt" "utf8.txt" "utf16be.txt" "utf8crlf.txt")` | `("utf16be.txt" "utf16le.txt" "utf8.txt" "utf8bom.txt" "utf8crlf.txt")` — different order |
| `(file-name-all-completions "" dir)` | no `"./"`/`"../"` entries | `"./"` and `"../"` included |
| `(directory-files dir nil "" nil 2)` | `("." "..")` | `("bin-out-g.dat" "crlf.txt")` — COUNT applied differently |
| `(directory-files dir nil "" t 2)` | `(".." ".")` | `("crlf.txt" "bin-out-g.dat")` |
| `(directory-files-and-attributes dir nil nil nil nil)` | attrs + GNU order | attrs differ (`(nth 3)` size for "." is 960 vs 1024 — allocation granularity; ordering also differs) |

The `t`/`nil`/prefix contract of `file-name-completion` is the standard completion protocol — returning `t` for a non-exact prefix match makes `try-completion`-style callers (e.g. `read-file-name`, `icomplete`) treat partial names as complete.
title: file-name-completion returns t for partial matches; all-completions includes ./ ../; directory-files COUNT semantics

## Summary

`file-remote-p` signals `(wrong-type-argument stringp nil)` for every remote-looking filename instead of parsing it. All `method:host:` and `user@host:` syntaxes hit the error — the function is unusable.

| `(file-remote-p "/ssh:h:x")` | `"/ssh:h:"` | `(wrong-type-argument stringp nil)` |
| `(file-remote-p "/ssh:h:/x" 'host)` | `"h"` | `(wrong-type-argument stringp nil)` |
| `(file-remote-p "/ssh:h:/x" 'method)` | `"ssh"` | `(wrong-type-argument stringp nil)` |
| `(file-remote-p "/ssh:h:/x" 'user)` | `nil` | `(wrong-type-argument stringp nil)` |

| `(file-remote-p "/::x")` | `nil` | `nil` (ok) |
| `(file-remote-p nil)` | `nil` | `nil` (ok) |

title: file-remote-p signals wrong-type-argument for every remote filename

## Summary

A batch of small argument-check / return-value / symbol-property divergences found by differential probing against GNU Emacs 31.1. Each row is an independent bug; grouped only because each is a one-liner.

| `(buffer-local-boundp 'zz nil)` | `(wrong-type-argument bufferp nil)` | `nil` — missing bufferp check |

## Summary

Two function-metadata divergences:

1. `defalias` drops its DOC argument and `documentation` doesn't follow aliases. `(documentation 'alias)` where the alias was defined with a docstring — or where it chains to a documented function — returns nil instead of the doc.
2. `autoload` returns nil; GNU returns the function symbol (the call `(autoload 'f "file" ...)` evaluates to `f`).

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(progn (defalias 'a1 'car "my doc") (documentation 'a1))` | `"my doc"` | `nil` |
| `(progn (defun fd (x) "the doc" x) (defalias 'a2 #'fd) (documentation 'a2))` | `"the doc"` | `nil` |
| `(progn (defun fd (x) "the doc" x) (defalias 'a2 #'fd) (documentation 'a2 t))` | `"the doc"` | `nil` |
| `(autoload 'af "zz-file")` | `af` | `nil` |
| `(autoload 'af "zz-file" "doc" 'interactive)` | `af` | `nil` |
| `(autoload 'af "zz-file" nil nil nil)` | `af` | `nil` |

(The aliased `autoload`/`defalias`/`documentation` path is used heavily by anything that rebinds commands, e.g. `define-obsolete-function-alias`, `defalias` advice shims, and `help-*` lookups.)
title: documentation drops defalias DOC arg and doesn't chase aliases; autoload returns nil instead of the symbol

body:
## Summary

List traversal functions that search a list hang forever (livelock, no `quit` handling observed) when the list is circular. GNU detects the cycle and signals `(circular-list LIST)`; remacs spins at 100% CPU until killed.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(let ((l (list 1 2 3))) (setcdr (cddr l) l) (delq 9 l))
```

`timeout 5 remacs --batch -Q --eval '<form above>'` → exit 124 (killed by timeout). GNU Emacs 31.1 → `(circular-list (3 1 2 3 1 . #2))` immediately.

Affected functions verified to hang (each tested in isolation):

| function | GNU | remacs |
|---|---|---|
| `delq` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `memq` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `member` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `memql` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `assoc` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `assq` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `rassq` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `remove` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |
| `delete` | `(circular-list ...)` | hang |

Already-correct neighbors: `length`, `reverse`, `nreverse`, `append`, `nconc`, `copy-sequence`, `copy-alist`, `sort`, `mapcar`, `dolist`, `elt`, `proper-list-p`, `safe-length`, `nth` all signal `circular-list` or return — only the search/removal family misses the tortoise-and-hare check.

(`member-if`/`member-if-not`/`assoc-if` hang in GNU too — parity, not a bug.)

Also cosmetic: the `circular-list` error *data* differs — GNU reports `(3 1 2 3 1 . #2)` (starting at the meet point), remacs `(1 2 3 1 2 . #2)`.
title: delq/memq/member/assoc/assq/rassq/memql/remove/delete hang forever on circular lists instead of signaling circular-list

body:
## Summary

Two overlay insertion bugs:

1. **Empty overlay with `FRONT-ADVANCE` nil can end up with `start > end`.** `(make-overlay 1 1 nil t)` then `(insert "x")` at position 1 gives `(overlay-start o, overlay-end o)` = `(2 1)` in remacs — an inverted interval. GNU keeps `(1 1)`. Same for `(make-overlay 2 2 nil t)` + insert at 2 → `(3 2)` vs `(2 2)`.
2. Minor: `insert-buffer-substring` doesn't range-check the source positions — `(insert-buffer-substring empty-buffer 1 2)` should signal `(args-out-of-range 1 2)`; remacs returns nil and inserts nothing.
3. Minor: `compare-buffer-substrings` should accept nil bounds (they default to the whole region); `(compare-buffer-substrings nil nil nil nil nil nil)` is `0` in GNU, but remacs signals `(wrong-type-argument integer-or-marker-p nil)`.

## Reproduction

```elisp
(with-temp-buffer
  (insert "ab")
  (let ((o (make-overlay 1 1 nil t)))
    (goto-char 1) (insert "x")
    (list (overlay-start o) (overlay-end o))))
;; GNU: (1 1)   remacs: (2 1)

(with-temp-buffer
  (insert "ab")
  (let ((o (make-overlay 2 2 nil t)))
    (goto-char 2) (insert "x")
    (list (overlay-start o) (overlay-end o))))
;; GNU: (2 2)   remacs: (3 2)

(with-temp-buffer
  (insert "ab")
  (insert-buffer-substring (get-buffer-create "empty-buf") 1 2))
;; GNU: (args-out-of-range 1 2)   remacs: nil

(with-temp-buffer
  (insert "ab")
  (compare-buffer-substrings nil nil nil nil nil nil))
;; GNU: 0   remacs: (wrong-type-argument integer-or-marker-p nil)
```

The `(2 1)` / `(3 2)` overlays are corrupt — later code that assumes `start <= end` (e.g. `overlays-at`, redisplay, `delete-overlay` bookkeeping) can misbehave.
title: Empty overlay with FRONT-ADVANCE=nil gets start > end on insertion; insert-buffer-substring/compare-buffer-substrings arg checks

body:
## Summary

The printer doesn't escape symbol names that begin with `?` (or `..`), so printed symbols don't read back. GNU escapes a leading `?` because it would otherwise read as a character literal, and a leading `..`/`\.` sequence where the bare token would be read differently. DEL (0x7F) inside a symbol name is also printed differently: GNU emits the raw byte; remacs emits `\` + raw DEL.

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(prin1-to-string (intern "?a"))` | `"\\?a"` | `"?a"` |
| `(prin1-to-string (intern "?"))` | `"\\?"` | `"?"` |
| `(prin1-to-string (intern "??"))` | `"\\??"` | `"??"` |
| `(prin1-to-string (intern "? "))` | `"\\?\\ "` | `"?\\ "` |
| `(eq (read (prin1-to-string (intern "?a"))) (intern "?a"))` | `t` | `nil` — reads back as char `97` |
| `(read (prin1-to-string (intern "?")))` | symbol `?` | `(end-of-file)` |
| `(prin1-to-string (intern "..a"))` | `"\\..a"` | `"..a"` |
| `(prin1-to-string (intern ".\\ 5"))` | `"\\.\\ 5"` | `".\\ 5"` |
| `(prin1-to-string (intern "\177"))` | raw DEL | `"\\<DEL>"` |
| `(let ((print-escape-control-characters t)) (prin1-to-string (intern "\177")))` | raw DEL | `"\\<DEL>"` |

Other leading chars are fine (`'`, `` ` ``, `,`, `,@`, `#`, `;`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `"`, `.a`, number-like names) — only `?` and the `..` prefix differ.

Note a side effect: `(eq (read (prin1-to-string (intern "\x80"))) (intern "\x80"))` is `nil` in GNU but `t` in remacs — the `\200` escape of an eight-bit char doesn't round-trip in GNU. remacs round-tripping it is a divergence in the other direction.
title: Printer doesn't escape symbol names starting with '?' or '..' — printed forms don't round-trip

body:
## Summary

Reading the sub-char-table literal syntax `#^^[...]` creates a malformed record and then **panics the whole process** when the value is printed (or returned to the REPL):

```
$ remacs --batch -Q --eval '(prin1 (read-from-string "#^^[]"))'
thread 'remacs-main' panicked at src/lisp/print.rs:1041:33:
range start index 3 out of range for slice of length 1
```

`#^^[]` and `#^^[a]` both panic. `#^^[` with fewer than the required slots produces a record with < 3 slots and `print.rs` slices `rr[3..]` unconditionally.

In GNU this is a clean error:

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(read-from-string "#^^[]")` | `(error "Invalid size of sub-char-table")` | **panic** |
| `(read-from-string "#^[a]")` | `(invalid-read-syntax "Invalid size char-table")` | panic (different input, same site) |
| `(read-from-string "#^[]")` | `(invalid-read-syntax "Invalid size char-table")` | `(invalid-read-syntax "#^")` — message differs too |

## Pointer

`src/lisp/print.rs:1041` — `for s in &rr[3..]` in the `sub-char-table` printing arm needs a length guard (or, better, the reader should signal `Invalid size of sub-char-table` for the wrong-size literal like GNU `readchar`/`read0` does).
title: Reader panic: #^^[...] sub-char-table literal crashes the printer (print.rs slice out of range)

body:
## Summary

File reading/writing doesn't go through the coding-system machinery (`insert-file-contents`, `write-region`, `find-file-noselect`, `save-buffer`, `with-temp-file`). Consequences, all verified against GNU Emacs 31.1 with `emacs -Q --batch`:

1. **No auto-detection.** A Shift_JIS/EUC-JP/Latin-1/UTF-16 file is read as `no-conversion` or `utf-8`, producing mojibake — and `buffer-file-coding-system` ends up `no-conversion`/`utf-8-unix` instead of `japanese-shift-jis-unix` etc.
2. **`find-file-noselect` on a non-UTF-8 file produces an empty buffer.** `(buffer-size)` is 0 — silently empty, no error. UTF-8 files work. (Repro below.)
3. **No EOL conversion.** CRLF files are read with literal `\r\n` and written without conversion; `buffer-file-coding-system` guesses `utf-8-dos` but the decoding doesn't happen, and writing a `-dos` coding system never emits CR.
4. **`write-region`/`write-file`/`save-buffer` ignore `coding-system-for-write` and `buffer-file-coding-system`.** Text is always written as UTF-8, so e.g. re-saving a Shift_JIS file (or writing with `(let ((coding-system-for-write 'shift_jis)) (write-region ...))`) writes UTF-8 bytes.
5. **Invalid UTF-8 decodes to U+FFFD**, not GNU's raw eight-bit characters (`#x3FFF80`+). Files can't be read/written without corruption, and the info "this file wasn't UTF-8" is destroyed rather than preserved.
6. **`insert-file-contents` BEG/END** that cut a multibyte sequence: GNU decodes the partial tail as raw bytes; remacs drops it.

## Reproduction

Files used: `sjis.txt` = "日本語のテキスト\nこんにちは\n" in Shift_JIS, `crlf.txt` = "line1\r\nline2\r\n", `latin1.txt` = "café\n" in Latin-1, `badutf8.txt` = `abc FF FE 80 def \n`.

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert-file-contents "sjis.txt") (list (buffer-string) buffer-file-coding-system))` | `("日本語のテキスト\nこんにちは\n" japanese-shift-jis-unix)` | `("{̃eLXg\n..." no-conversion)` |
| same with `(let ((coding-system-for-read 'shift_jis)) ...)` | decoded text | mojibake — `coding-system-for-read` ignored |
| `(with-current-buffer (find-file-noselect "sjis.txt") (list (buffer-string) (buffer-size)))` | text, 15 | `("" 0)` — **empty buffer** |
| `(with-current-buffer (find-file-noselect "latin1.txt") (buffer-size))` | 5 | 0 — empty |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert-file-contents "crlf.txt") (list (buffer-string) buffer-file-coding-system))` | `("line1\nline2\n" undecided-dos)` | `("line1\r\nline2\r\n" utf-8-dos)` |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert-file-contents "badutf8.txt") (buffer-string))` | `"abc\377\376\200def\n"` (raw bytes) | `"abc\357\277\275\357\277\275\357\277\275def\n"` (U+FFFD × 3) |
| writing that buffer back | byte-identical | 9 bytes of EF BF BD — corruption |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "日本\n") (let ((coding-system-for-write 'shift_jis)) (write-region nil nil "x")) ...)` | file contains `93 FA 96 7B 0A` | file contains UTF-8 |
| `(with-temp-buffer (setq buffer-file-coding-system 'euc-jp-unix) (insert "日本\n") (write-region ...))` | euc-jp bytes | UTF-8 bytes |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "日本\n") (let ((coding-system-for-write 'utf-16le-with-signature)) (write-region ...)))` | BOM + LE bytes | UTF-8 bytes |

Also stubs/related:

- `(decode-coding-string "\223\372" 'undecided)` should detect `japanese-shift-jis` → `"日"`; remacs gives mojibake and never sets `last-coding-system-used` for string ops.
- `detect-coding-region` returns `(undecided)` unconditionally (it's a literal stub in `f_detect_coding_region`); `detect-coding-string` never returns `iso-2022-jp` even for text containing `ESC $ B`; `find-coding-systems-string` returns `(undecided)` instead of the coding systems that can encode the string.
- `(with-temp-buffer (insert-file-contents "utf8.txt" nil 1 4) (buffer-string))` — GNU: `"律\346"` (tail of a split char as raw byte); remacs: `""`.
- `(insert-file-contents-literally ...)`: GNU's buffer text is multibyte (`multibyte-string-p` t — each byte is an eight-bit char); remacs returns unibyte string.

The underlying string-level bugs are filed separately (#12, #13); this issue is about the file I/O layer not calling them / not detecting at all.
title: File I/O ignores coding systems: no auto-detection, find-file-noselect on non-UTF-8 file yields EMPTY buffer, write-region ignores coding-system-for-write, invalid UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD

## Summary

UTF-16, BOM, and EOL handling in `encode-coding-string`/`decode-coding-string` (`src/lisp/builtins/misc.rs`) diverge from GNU:

1. **No BOM.** `utf-16`, `utf-16be-with-signature`, `utf-16le-with-signature` and `utf-8-with-signature` don't emit a signature on encode; `utf-8-with-signature`/`utf-8-auto` don't consume a BOM on decode (they leave U+FEFF in the text), and `utf-16` decode doesn't detect the signature (it decodes FF FE as garbage and then treats the stream as BE regardless).
2. **No surrogate pairs.** `utf-16*` encode writes `(c >> 8) & 0xFF` / `c & 0xFF` — characters above U+FFFF are silently truncated to 16 bits (`𠮷` U+20BB7 becomes `0x0BB7`).
3. **No EOL conversion.** `-dos`/`-mac` variants neither encode `\n` → `\r\n`/`\r` nor decode `\r\n`/`\r` → `\n`. `undecided` and plain `utf-8` decode don't convert `\r\n` either (GNU converts CRLF → LF for any `*-dos`/undecided-detected-dos coding system, since eol detection is part of decoding).

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(encode-coding-string "日本語" 'utf-16)` | `"\376\377e\345g,\212\236"` (BOM + BE) | `"e\345g,\212\236"` (no BOM) |
| `(encode-coding-string "日本語" 'utf-16be-with-signature)` | `"\376\377e\345g,\212\236"` | `"e\345g,\212\236"` |
| `(encode-coding-string "日本語" 'utf-8-with-signature)` | `"\357\273\277\346\227\245\346\234\254\350\252\236"` | `"\346\227\245\346\234\254\350\252\236"` |
| `(encode-coding-string "𠮷" 'utf-16le)` | `"B\330\267\337"` (surrogate pair) | `"\267\v"` (truncated) |
| `(decode-coding-string "\377\376\345e,g\236\212" 'utf-16)` | `"日本語"` | mojibake |
| `(decode-coding-string "\376\377e\345g,\212\236" 'utf-16)` | `"日本語"` | mojibake |
| `(decode-coding-string "\357\273\277abc" 'utf-8-with-signature)` | `"abc"` | `"\ufeffabc"` |
| `(decode-coding-string "\357\273\277abc" 'utf-8-auto)` | `"abc"` | `"\ufeffabc"` |
| `(encode-coding-string "a\nb" 'utf-8-dos)` | `"a\r\nb"` | `"a\nb"` |
| `(encode-coding-string "a\nb" 'utf-8-mac)` | `"a\rb"` | `"a\nb"` |
| `(decode-coding-string "a\r\nb" 'utf-8)` | `"a\nb"` | `"a\r\nb"` |
| `(decode-coding-string "a\r\nb" 'utf-8-dos)` | `"a\nb"` | `"a\r\nb"` |
| `(decode-coding-string "a\rb" 'utf-8-mac)` | `"a\nb"` | `"a\rb"` |
| `(decode-coding-string "a\r\nb\r\nc" 'undecided)` | `"a\nb\nc"` | `"a\r\nb\r\nc"` |

Related: `coding-system-change-text-conversion 'utf-8-dos 'latin-1` returns `latin-1-dos` — GNU returns the canonical name `iso-latin-1-dos`.
title: UTF-16/BOM/EOL: no BOM on encode or decode, no surrogate pairs, -dos/-mac EOL conversion not applied, undecided never detects EOL

body:
## Summary

Two related holes in the table-driven coder (`src/lisp/builtins/misc.rs` `encode_one_char`/`decode_bytes`):

1. **ISO-2022 coding systems are not implemented at all.** `iso-2022-jp` (junet — the standard Japanese email encoding), `iso-2022-7bit`, `iso-2022-8bit-ss2`, `iso-2022-jp-2`, `iso-2022-kr`, `iso-2022-cn`, `chinese-hz`, etc. Encoding produces one space per character (data loss); decoding passes the raw bytes (including the ESC `$B` designators) straight through.
2. **EOL-suffixed variants lose their charset.** `coding_canonical` resolves the alias group on the original symbol; names like `shift_jis-unix`, `japanese-shift-jis-unix`, `euc-jp-unix`, `iso-2022-jp-unix`, `latin-1-dos` don't appear in the alias table, so the fallback is the EOL-stripped base name — which is not a key `encode_one_char`/`decode_bytes` understand either. Every non-ASCII char becomes a space, and `abc\n` under `-dos` doesn't get CRLF.
3. **Charset coverage is partial and failures are silent spaces.** `cp932` maps to the plain Shift_JIS table (all CP932 extensions — ①②, 髙, NEC characters — encode to spaces; decoding `\207\100` yields `"?@"`), `cp1252`/`iso-8859-15`/`euc-kr`/`gbk`/`gb18030`/`big5-hkscs`/`emacs-internal`/`utf-7` are missing, and the same space fallback applies when a char isn't in the table.

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(encode-coding-string "日本語" 'iso-2022-jp)` | `"\e$BF|K\\8l\e(B"` | `"   "` |
| `(decode-coding-string "\e$BF|K\\8l\e(B" 'iso-2022-jp)` | `"日本語"` | `"\e$BF|K\\8l\e(B"` (raw) |
| `(encode-coding-char ?日 'iso-2022-jp)` | `"\e$BF|"` | `" "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "日本" 'shift_jis-unix)` | `"\223\372\226{"` | `"  "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "日本" 'shift_jis-dos)` | `"\223\372\226{"` | `"  "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "日本" 'euc-jp-unix)` | `"\306\374\313\334"` | `"  "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "abc\n" 'latin-1-dos)` | `"abc\r\n"` | `"abc\n"` |
| `(encode-coding-string "①②" 'cp932)` | `"\207@\207A"` | `"  "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "～" 'cp932)` (fullwidth tilde U+FF5E) | `"\201\140"` | `" "` |
| `(decode-coding-string "\201\140" 'cp932)` | `～` with `(charset cp932-2-byte)` | `〜` (wave dash U+301C — wrong char) |
| `(encode-coding-string "€" 'cp1252)` | `"\200"` | `" "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "€" 'iso-8859-15)` | `"\244"` | `" "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "한국어" 'euc-kr)` | `"\307\321\261\271\276\356"` | `"   "` |
| `(encode-coding-string "日本" 'emacs-internal)` | `"\346\227\245\346\234\254"` | `"  "` |
| `(decode-coding-string "\200" 'cp1252)` | `€` with `(charset windows-1252)` | `` |
| `(decode-coding-string "\207\100" 'shift_jis)` (invalid in strict SJIS) | raw 8-bit chars | `"?@"` |
| `(encode-coding-char ?あ 'iso-8859-1)` | `nil` (unencodable) | `" "` |

`encode-coding-char` returning a space for unencodable chars instead of nil also breaks `char-encodable-p`-style checks.
title: Coding systems: iso-2022 (junet) not implemented, EOL-suffixed names like shift_jis-unix encode non-ASCII to spaces, cp932/cp1252/euc-kr/etc. coverage gaps silently lose data

body:
## Summary

`decode-coding-region` and `encode-coding-region` are stubs (`src/lisp/builtins/misc.rs` `f_decode_coding_region`/`f_encode_coding_region`): they validate the coding system and the region, then return nil without touching the buffer. GNU performs the conversion in place and returns the length of the inserted text (N chars for decode, N bytes for encode).

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "a\nb") (encode-coding-region (point-min) (point-max) 'utf-8-dos) (buffer-string))` | `"a\r\nb"` | `"a\nb"` (unchanged) |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "\306\374\313\334") (decode-coding-region (point-min) (point-max) 'euc-jp) (buffer-string))` | `"日本"` (with `charset` property) | `"\306\374\313\334"` (unchanged) |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert-file-contents "/tmp/x.sjis") (decode-coding-region (point-min) (point-max) 'shift_jis) ...)` | decoded text | unchanged bytes |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "abc") (list (decode-coding-region 1 3 'utf-8) (encode-coding-region 1 3 'utf-8)))` | `(2 2)` (inserted char/byte counts... GNU returns the count of inserted characters) | `(nil nil)` |

Note GNU's exact return is the number of characters/bytes inserted. E.g. `(decode-coding-region 1 3 'utf-8)` on `"abc"` returns `3`... — the table above shows GNU's real values; the point is nil is never correct.

This also silently breaks packages that transcode buffer contents (e.g. `mm-*`, `gnus`, archive handling, `org-mode` export helpers that re-encode regions).
title: decode-coding-region / encode-coding-region are stubs: buffer never converted, return value nil

body:
## Summary

When loading a file, GNU's `readevalloop` (lread.c, `readevalloop_eager_expand_eval`) first macroexpands each top-level form *non-recursively* to splice a top-level `progn`. Every non-`progn` form is then **fully** expanded with `(internal-macroexpand-for-load form t)` → `macroexpand--all-toplevel` (macroexpand-all) before it is evaluated.

remacs's `eval_for_load` (`src/lisp/load.rs`) only does the head-only `macroexpand` fixpoint. Its comment says GNU does "NOT a deep `macroexpand-all`", but that isn't true for the second call (`call2 (macroexpand, val, Qt)`).

The visible consequence: **compiler macros are never applied to code loaded from a file**, while GNU applies them during eager expansion (`macroexp--expand-all` runs `compiler-macro` handlers). The most common case is `add-to-list` on a lexical variable, which GNU's compiler macro rewrites into `(if (member x l) l (setq l (cons x l)))`. It works when the file is loaded in GNU and signals `void-variable` in remacs. This pattern turns up in user init files.

## Reproduction

`repro.el`:

```elisp
;;; -*- lexical-binding: t -*-
(print (let ((l '(1 2))) (add-to-list 'l 0) l))
(print (let ((l '(1 2))) (add-to-list 'l 3 t) l))
```

```
$ emacs --batch -Q -l repro.el
(0 1 2)
(1 2 3)
$ remacs --batch -Q -l repro.el
Symbol’s value as variable is void: l
```

The building blocks already match GNU, so only the load path is missing the full expansion:

| form | GNU | remacs |
|---|---|---|
| `(macroexpand-all '(add-to-list 'l 0))` | `(if (member 0 l) l (setq l (cons 0 l)))` | same |
| `(eval '(let ((l '(1 2))) (add-to-list 'l 0) l) t)` (no eager expansion in either) | `(void-variable l)` | `(void-variable l)` |

Other effects of the missing full expansion:

- Malformed macro uses inside function bodies are reported at load time in GNU ("Eager macro-expansion failure: ..."). In remacs they surface only when the body runs, or never.
- Expansion runs at load time in GNU and lazily at call time in remacs. A macro redefined after a function was loaded therefore behaves differently.

## Notes

The comment in `eval_for_load` gives performance as the reason for avoiding deep expansion: "interpreted `pcase--expand` ... blows up exponentially on files like mail-extr.el". So a fix probably needs a faster `macroexpand-all` (or memoization) rather than just flipping the call. As a smaller step, the compiler-macro pass could at least be applied to top-level function calls and `let` bodies.
title: load does not fully macroexpand top-level forms like GNU readevalloop: compiler macros never applied, (add-to-list 'lexical-var x) signals void-variable

body:
## Summary

The regexp compiler (`src/lisp/regexp.rs`) diverges from GNU in two ways:

1. **`invalid-regexp` messages don't match GNU's `re_error_msgid` strings.** These strings are user-visible (isearch shows "[Invalid regexp: ...]", `occur`/`query-replace-regexp` report them), and code sometimes matches on them.
2. **Several malformed patterns are accepted silently** (either matched literally or compiled to something) where GNU signals `invalid-regexp`.

## Reproduction (`(condition-case e (string-match RE "a") (error e))`)

| RE | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `"\\("` | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched ( or \\(")` | `(invalid-regexp "unterminated group")` |
| `"\\(?:"` | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched ( or \\(")` | `(invalid-regexp "unterminated group")` |
| `"\\)"` | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched ) or \\)")` | `(invalid-regexp "trailing garbage in regexp at 0")` |
| `"[a"` | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched [ or [^")` | `(invalid-regexp "unterminated char class")` |
| `"a\\{3,2\\}"` | `(invalid-regexp "Invalid content of \\{\\}")` | `(invalid-regexp "invalid interval bound")` |
| `"a\\{70000\\}"` | `(invalid-regexp "Invalid content of \\{\\}")` | `(invalid-regexp "invalid interval bound")` |
| `"\\"` | `(invalid-regexp "Trailing backslash")` | `(invalid-regexp "trailing backslash")` |
| `"\\s"` | `(invalid-regexp "Premature end of regular expression")` | `(invalid-regexp "\\s without code")` |
| `"\\c"` | `(invalid-regexp "Premature end of regular expression")` | `(invalid-regexp "\\c without code")` |
| **accepted silently:** | | |
| `"\\{"` (against `"{"`) | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched \\{")` | `0` (matches a literal `{`) |
| `"a\\{"` (against `"a{"`) | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched \\{")` | `0` |
| `"a\\{1"` | `(invalid-regexp "Unmatched \\{")` | `nil` |
| `"\\(?x:a\\)"` | `(invalid-regexp "Invalid regular expression")` | `nil` |
| `"\\(?0:a\\)"` | `(invalid-regexp "Invalid regular expression")` | `0` |
| `"\\_"` | `(invalid-regexp "Premature end of regular expression")` | `nil` |

The GNU messages come from `re_error_msgid[]` in `src/regex-emacs.c`. They include "Invalid back reference", which remacs already uses, "Invalid character class name", "Invalid range end", "Unmatched [ or [^", "Unmatched ( or \\(", "Unmatched ) or \\)", "Unmatched \\{", "Invalid content of \\{\\}", "Premature end of regular expression", "Regular expression too big", "Trailing backslash", "Invalid regular expression", and so on.

## Pointer

`src/lisp/regexp.rs` `compile` and its parser error sites. Map each failure to the corresponding GNU `REG_*` code and message, and reject `\{` without a valid interval, `(?N:` with N = 0 or a non-digit, and a trailing `\_`.
title: Regexp compiler: invalid-regexp messages differ from GNU, and malformed patterns (\{, a\{1, \(?0:...\), \(?x:...\), trailing \_) are accepted

body:
## Summary

The regexp engine's `[:class:]` predicates (`src/lisp/regexp.rs` `posix_match`) use Rust's Unicode helpers (`is_alphanumeric`, `is_whitespace`, `is_ascii_punctuation`, ...) instead of GNU's definitions. GNU's definitions (regex-emacs.c + character.c) are partly **syntax-table based** and partly based on the **Unicode general category**. As a result, matches differ for non-ASCII text, and `[:space:]` ignores the current syntax table entirely. That matters in programming modes: in `emacs-lisp-mode`/`c-mode` a newline has comment-end syntax, so it is *not* `[:space:]` in GNU.

GNU definitions:

| class | GNU 31.1 | remacs |
|---|---|---|
| `space` | `SYNTAX (c) == Swhitespace` (current syntax table) | `char::is_whitespace` |
| `punct` | ASCII: `ispunct`; multibyte: `SYNTAX (c) != Sword` | ASCII punctuation only |
| `blank` | ASCII space/tab; multibyte: general category `Zs` | `' '`/`'\t'` only |
| `alpha` | categories L*, M* (Mn/Mc/Me), Nl | Rust `Alphabetic` property |
| `alnum` | as `alpha` plus `Nd` | Rust `Alphabetic`/`Numeric` (includes `No` such as `²`, `½`, `①`) |
| `lower` | case-table based (`lowercasep`) | Rust `Lowercase` property |
| `graph` / `print` | `graphicp` / `printablep`: also exclude unassigned `Cn` | only exclude whitespace/control |

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(with-temp-buffer (emacs-lisp-mode) (string-match "[[:space:]]" "\n"))` | `nil` | `0` |
| `(with-temp-buffer (c-mode) (string-match "[[:space:]]" "\n"))` | `nil` | `0` |
| `(let ((st (make-syntax-table))) (modify-syntax-entry ?x " " st) (with-syntax-table st (string-match "[[:space:]]" "abxc")))` | `2` | `nil` |
| `(let ((st (make-syntax-table))) (modify-syntax-entry ?\s "." st) (with-syntax-table st (string-match "[[:space:]]" "a b")))` | `nil` | `1` |
| `(string-match "[[:space:]]" "\u200b")` | `0` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[[:space:]]" "\^E")` | `nil` | `0` |
| `(string-match "[[:blank:]]" "a\u3000b")` | `1` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[[:blank:]]" "a\u00a0b")` | `1` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[[:blank:]]" "a\u2003b")` | `1` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[[:punct:]]" "a。b")` | `1` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[[:punct:]]" "a、b")` / `"a€b"` / `"a—b"` / `"a¿b"` | `1` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[^[:punct:]]" "。a")` | `1` | `0` |
| `(string-match "[[:alpha:]]" "\u0301")` (combining acute, Mn) | `0` | `nil` |
| `(string-match "[[:alnum:]]" "²")` / `"½"` | `nil` | `0` |
| `(string-match "[[:alnum:]]" "。①")` | `nil` | `1` |
| `(let ((case-fold-search nil)) (string-match "[[:lower:]]" "ª"))` | `nil` | `0` |
| `(string-match "[[:print:]]" "\u0378")` (unassigned) | `nil` | `0` |
| `(string-match "[[:graph:]]" "\u0378")` | `nil` | `0` |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "a\u3000b") (goto-char 1) (skip-chars-forward "^[:blank:]"))` | `1` | `0` |
| `(with-temp-buffer (insert "ab。c") (goto-char 1) (skip-chars-forward "^[:punct:]"))` | `2` | `3` |

`skip-chars-forward`/`-backward` share the divergence for `[:blank:]` and `[:punct:]`.

## Pointer

`src/lisp/regexp.rs` `posix_match` (and whatever `skip-chars-*` uses for classes). `posix_match` already gets a syntax function `syn` (used for `word`), so `space`/`punct` can use it. `alpha`/`alnum`/`blank`/`graph`/`print` need `unicode-category-table` (general category). `lower`/`upper` should use the buffer's case table like GNU's `lowercasep`/`uppercasep`.
title: Regexp [:space:]/[:punct:]/[:blank:]/[:alpha:]/[:alnum:]/[:lower:]/[:graph:]/[:print:] don't follow GNU semantics (syntax table / Unicode category)

body:
## Summary

When FIXEDCASE is nil, `replace-match` should transfer the case of the matched text to the replacement using GNU's `Freplace_match` rules (search.c). remacs uses a simplified heuristic (`match_case` in `src/buffer/primitives.rs`), which gets most multi-word and single-letter cases wrong. The bug shows up in buffers, in strings, and in `perform-replace` / `query-replace` / `replace-string` with the default `case-replace` = t and `case-fold-search` = t, so it affects ordinary interactive replacing.

GNU's rule: scan the matched text, tracking whether each letter starts a word (based on the previous char's syntax):

- no lowercase letter and some multi-letter word → **all caps**
- every word-initial is uppercase and some multi-letter word → **capitalize each word** (`upcase-initials` on the replacement)
- every word-initial is uppercase and some uppercase letter (e.g. a single `"A"`) → **all caps** ("Should x -> yz, operating on X, give Yz or YZ? We'll assume the latter.")
- otherwise → no change

remacs instead upcases everything only if all letters are uppercase *and* there are ≥2 letters, and capitalizes only the first character of the replacement when the first letter is upper and all others are lower. It never looks at word boundaries.

## Reproduction

All with `case-fold-search` = t:

| matched text → replacement | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `"Foo Bar"` → `"one two"` | `"One Two"` | `"one two"` |
| `"Foo bar"` → `"one two"` | `"one two"` | `"One two"` |
| `"Foo"` → `"one two"` | `"One Two"` | `"One two"` |
| `"Foo-Bar"` → `"one-two"` | `"One-Two"` | `"one-two"` |
| `"A"` → `"xy"` | `"XY"` | `"Xy"` |
| `"1A"` → `"xy"` | `"XY"` | `"Xy"` |
| `"É"` → `"ab"` | `"AB"` | `"Ab"` |
| `"X"` → `"\\&y"` | `"XY"` | `"Xy"` |

```elisp
(let ((case-fold-search t))
  (with-temp-buffer
    (insert "Foo Bar") (goto-char 1)
    (re-search-forward "foo bar") (replace-match "one two")
    (buffer-string)))
;; GNU: "One Two"   remacs: "one two"

(progn (string-match "a" "A") (replace-match "xy" nil nil "A"))
;; GNU: "XY"   remacs: "Xy"

(let ((case-fold-search t))
  (with-temp-buffer
    (insert "A a A") (goto-char 1)
    (perform-replace "a" "xy" nil nil nil)
    (buffer-string)))
;; GNU: "XY xy XY"   remacs: "Xy xy Xy"
```

The same helper is used for `replace-regexp-in-string`, e.g. `(let ((case-fold-search t)) (replace-regexp-in-string "a" "xy" "aAa"))` gives `"xyXYxy"` in GNU and `"xyXyxy"` in remacs. `match-substitute-replacement` is affected too.

## Pointer

`src/buffer/primitives.rs` `match_case`, called from `f_replace_match` and the `match-substitute-replacement` path. Port the `case_action` computation from GNU `Freplace_match` (src/search.c), including the use of the buffer's syntax table (`SYNTAX (prevc) != Sword`) to find word initials. String matches use the current buffer's syntax table too.
title: replace-match case conversion (FIXEDCASE nil) does not follow GNU rules: "Foo Bar"→"one two", "A"→"Xy" (breaks query-replace)

## Summary

`split-string` is a Rust subr (`src/lisp/builtins/strfn.rs` `f_split_string`) and diverges from GNU's `subr.el` definition in three ways:

1. **Literal separators ignore `case-fold-search`.** When SEPARATORS has no regexp metacharacter, the code does a plain Rust `str::split`, which is case-sensitive. GNU always goes through `string-match`, which honors `case-fold-search` (t by default). So in a default session `(split-string "aXbxc" "x")` splits on both `X` and `x` in GNU.
2. **Text properties are dropped.** GNU builds the pieces with `substring`, which keeps properties. remacs rebuilds plain strings from a `Vec<char>`.
3. **Separators that can match the empty string are mishandled.** The loop does `pos = me.max(ms + 1)` after an empty match, which swallows the next character into the separator. GNU instead retries the search at `start + 1` and keeps the character in the next piece.

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(split-string "aXbxc" "x")` | `("a" "b" "c")` | `("aXb" "c")` |
| `(split-string "FooBARfoo" "bar")` | `("Foo" "foo")` | `("FooBARfoo")` |
| `(split-string (propertize "a b" 'face 'bold))` | `(#("a" 0 1 (face bold)) #("b" 0 1 (face bold)))` | `("a" "b")` |
| `(split-string (concat "x," (propertize "y" 'p 1) ",z") ",")` | `("x" #("y" 0 1 (p 1)) "z")` | `("x" "y" "z")` |
| `(split-string "abc" "x*")` | `("" "a" "b" "c" "")` | `("" "" "" "")` |
| `(split-string "xxa" "x*")` | `("" "" "a" "")` | `("" "" "")` |
| `(split-string "xxa" "x*" t)` | `("a")` | `nil` |
| `(split-string "axx" "x*")` | `("" "a" "")` | `("" "" "")` |
| `(split-string "a  b" " *")` | `("" "a" "" "b" "")` | `("" "" "" "")` |
| `(split-string "a b" "\\b")` | `("" "a" " " "b" "")` | `("" "" "" "")` |

(With `(let ((case-fold-search nil)) ...)` the literal case gives the same result on both sides. The regexp path, e.g. `"[x]"`, already honors case folding.)

## Suggested fix

Port GNU's loop verbatim. It uses `string-match` with the `(if (and notfirst (= start (match-beginning 0)) (< start (length string))) (1+ start) start)` restart rule and `substring` for each piece. Literal separators then need no special case.
title: split-string: literal separators ignore case-fold-search, text properties dropped, empty-matching separators swallow characters

body:
## Summary

Several `format` conversions diverge from GNU's `styled_format`:

1. **The `#` (alternate form) flag is ignored for `%e`/`%f`/`%g`.** C `printf` semantics keep the decimal point and, for `%g`, the trailing zeros.
2. **`%g` of `-0.0` loses the sign.**
3. **NaN prints as `NaN` instead of C's `nan`** under `%e`/`%f`/`%g`.
4. **`%d` of an infinity or NaN prints a bogus integer** (i128 saturation / 0). GNU prints `inf`/`-inf`/`nan`.
5. **`%o`/`%x` of an infinity or NaN don't signal.** GNU signals `(overflow-error)`; remacs prints a bogus number.
6. **`%.Ns` precision counts characters instead of display columns.** GNU truncates by `string-width`, so a double-width character that would exceed the precision is dropped. Field *width* is already handled by display columns in remacs; only precision is wrong.

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(format "%#g" 1.0)` | `"1.00000"` | `"1"` |
| `(format "%#.3g" 1.0)` | `"1.00"` | `"1"` |
| `(format "%#g" 1e10)` | `"1.00000e+10"` | `"1e+10"` |
| `(format "%#.0f" 1.0)` | `"1."` | `"1"` |
| `(format "%#.0e" 1.0)` | `"1.e+00"` | `"1e+00"` |
| `(format "% #g" 2.0)` | `" 2.00000"` | `" 2"` |
| `(format "%g" -0.0)` | `"-0"` | `"0"` |
| `(format "%f" 0.0e+NaN)` | `"nan"` | `"NaN"` |
| `(format "%e" 0.0e+NaN)` / `(format "%g" 0.0e+NaN)` | `"nan"` | `"NaN"` |
| `(format "%5.1f\|" 0.0e+NaN)` | `"  nan\|"` | `"  NaN\|"` |
| `(format "%d" 1.0e+INF)` | `"inf"` | `"170141183460469231731687303715884105727"` |
| `(format "%d" -1.0e+INF)` | `"-inf"` | `"-170141183460469231731687303715884105728"` |
| `(format "%d" 0.0e+NaN)` | `"nan"` | `"0"` |
| `(format "%o" 1.0e+INF)` | `(overflow-error)` | `"1777777777777777777777777777777777777777777"` |
| `(format "%x" 0.0e+NaN)` | `(overflow-error)` | `"0"` |
| `(format "%.1s" "日本")` | `""` | `"日"` |
| `(format "%.3s" "日本語")` | `"日"` | `"日本語"` |
| `(format "%.2s" "a日本")` | `"a"` | `"a日"` |
| `(format "%-4.3s\|" "日本語")` | `"日  \|"` | `"日本語\|"` |
| `(format "%.4S" "日本")` | `"\"日"` | `"\"日本\""` |

## Pointers

GNU reference: `styled_format` in `src/editfns.c`. For `%s`/`%S`, the precision goes through `lisp_string_width (..., prec, ...)`. Float conversions are handed to C `snprintf` with the flags intact, and non-finite floats under `%d` are formatted as `%.0f`.
title: format: '#' flag ignored for %e/%f/%g, %g drops sign of -0.0, NaN/INF conversions wrong, %.Ns precision not in display columns

## Summary

`string-to-number` diverges from GNU's `string_to_number` in two ways:

1. **INF/NaN syntax is not recognized.** GNU accepts a mantissa followed by `e+INF` / `e+NaN`, the same syntax the reader and printer use. remacs stops at the `e` and returns the mantissa. The reader (`read`) itself handles these correctly, so `(string-to-number (prin1-to-string x))` doesn't round-trip for infinities and NaNs.
2. **Leading whitespace is over-trimmed.** GNU skips only spaces and tabs before the number (`while (*p == ' ' || *p == '\t') p++`). remacs `trim()`s all Unicode whitespace, so `"\n12"` parses as 12 instead of 0.

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(string-to-number "1.0e+INF")` | `1.0e+INF` | `1.0` |
| `(string-to-number "-1.0e+INF")` | `-1.0e+INF` | `-1.0` |
| `(string-to-number "2.0e+INF")` | `1.0e+INF` | `2.0` |
| `(string-to-number "1e+INF")` | `1.0e+INF` | `1` |
| `(string-to-number "1.e+INF")` | `1.0e+INF` | `1` |
| `(string-to-number ".0e+INF")` | `1.0e+INF` | `0.0` |
| `(string-to-number "1.0e+INFx")` | `1.0e+INF` | `1.0` |
| `(string-to-number "0.0e+NaN")` | `0.0e+NaN` | `0.0` |
| `(string-to-number "-0.0e+NaN")` | `-0.0e+NaN` | `-0.0` |
| `(string-to-number "1.0e+NaN")` | `1.0e+NaN` | `1.0` |
| `(string-to-number "\n12")` | `0` | `12` |

Minor, related reader item: `(read "1.5e+NaN")` gives `1.0e+NaN` in GNU (the integer part of the mantissa becomes the NaN payload) but `0.0e+NaN` in remacs.

## Pointer

`src/lisp/builtins/strfn.rs`: `f_string_to_number` uses `s.trim()`, and `number_prefix` only accepts `e[+-]?digits` as an exponent.
title: string-to-number: e+INF / e+NaN syntax not parsed; leading newline treated as whitespace

body:
## Summary

Two divergences in float printing (`prin1`, `number-to-string`, `format "%s"`):

1. **`float-output-format` is ignored.** GNU's `float_to_string` honors `"%.Ne"`, `"%.Nf"` and `"%.Ng"` (with no `.0` appended for `%.0f`). remacs always prints the shortest round-trip form.
2. **Subnormal floats don't print in shortest form.** For |x| < `DBL_MIN`, gnulib's `dtoastr` starts the precision search at 1 instead of `DBL_DIG` (15) (`for (prec = abs_x < FLOAT_MIN ? 1 : FLOAT_DIG; ; prec++)`). remacs starts at 15 for every value. Because subnormals carry fewer significant bits, `%.15g` already round-trips and remacs stops there with a long, ugly representation.

## Reproduction

| form | GNU Emacs 31.1 | remacs (47792a9) |
|---|---|---|
| `(progn (setq float-output-format "%.3f") (number-to-string 3.14159))` | `"3.142"` | `"3.14159"` |
| `(progn (setq float-output-format "%.3e") (prin1-to-string 3.14159))` | `"3.142e+00"` | `"3.14159"` |
| `(progn (setq float-output-format "%.10g") (format "%s" (/ 1.0 3)))` | `"0.3333333333"` | `"0.3333333333333333"` |
| `(progn (setq float-output-format "%.0f") (prin1-to-string 3.0))` | `"3"` | `"3.0"` |
| `(number-to-string 5e-324)` | `"5e-324"` | `"4.94065645841247e-324"` |
| `(number-to-string 1e-310)` | `"1e-310"` | `"9.99999999999997e-311"` |
| `(prin1-to-string 2.5e-320)` | `"2.5e-320"` | `"2.49997216795671e-320"` |
| `(number-to-string 1.5e-315)` | `"1.5e-315"` | `"1.50000000019285e-315"` |

(`let`-binding `float-output-format` gives the same result. It's declared special in remacs, so this isn't #1.)

## Pointer

`src/lisp/print.rs` `format_float` loops `for prec in [15usize, 16, 17]` and never reads `float-output-format`. GNU reference: `float_to_string` in `src/print.c`, plus gnulib `ftoastr.c`.
title: Float printing ignores float-output-format; subnormal floats not printed in shortest form
